records.title: Show HN: Four LLMs play 20 questions for real money, live
records.author: Individuum
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I wanted to explore how AI models behave when they have their own money. So I gave 4 frontier models their own USDC and had them compete in games of 20 questions. Anyone can watch live.

Each round, one model takes a turn picking the secret word, and the others interrogate it in a group chat.

Every move costs money: 10 cents to ask a question, $1.00 for a wrong guess, and a right guess takes the pot.

Questions are paid for privately, but inform everyone. This introduces a free rider problem that's fun to observe.

The models privately record their best guess and confidence level on every turn. This makes it possible to look for patterns in how they’re calibrated.

Overconfident models bleed money, timid ones rarely win, and well-calibrated ones get rich.

The money is real, and every transfer is on-chain.

At the end of each game a referee model judges the transcript to make sure the host didn’t lie in any answers. If the host is caught lying, it forfeits all its fees (it happens).

Season 1 ran for 85 games and Gemini turned $25 into $61 while Claude and Grok went broke.

Models who had recently guessed wrong were 5x more likely to guess again. Full writeup at https://aquarium.money/twenty/about

Season 2 is live now, and you can watch them play here: https://aquarium.money/twenty

Built solo as a side project.

records.storyText:
Claude Code's scheduled tasks (routines) leaves a session behind on every run and in the desktop app you can only delete them one at a time. We had 618 open sessions in just one routine.

The skill plans the clean up (keeps the newest N and protect any sessions where you typed a reply - optional) and then has Claude delete through the apps own session tool, 25 per call each behind an approval card.

The planner is a single python file that dosnt delete by itself so you can run it by hand to see where everything exists.

records.title: Show HN: Terminal Gym – a Claude mod that makes you do pushups between prompts
records.author: heynaitik
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I built this for myself and wanted to open-source it.

The problem: I wanted a way to get reminders in-between prompts as I often spend long hours in the terminal, especially now that we're usually parallel-processing so many agents.

The first version was a simple rep counter in my Claude Code status line and a shell script to log reps. Since Claude Code shipped mods this week, I thought this was a good way to level it up with even more accountability.

How it works: 1. Every day, you get a daily goal for either squats, pushups, or dips (e.g. 0/100 pushups) with +5 / +10 / +25 buttons to log a set in the terminal. 2. Reminders for sets are spread out across the day so it doesn't get annoying, starting from your first prompt for the day. A toast tells you when the next set is due. 3. Strict mode is opt-in: if you're falling behind in terms of your daily rep goal, it will block your prompts till you log some reps.

Added a streak counter for some added fun. All local and data is stored as plain files in ~/.claude/fitness.

Install: claude plugin marketplace add DrumAndCode/terminal-gym && claude plugin install terminal-gym@terminal-gym

Overall, thought the mod API is super powerful and can't wait to see the stuff people build with it. Eg: I built a clickable onboarding process inside the terminal, and that felt quite powerful to use.

Now you can enjoy spending both tokens and calories. :)

records.title: Show HN: AstroHelm – Use your phone camera to aim a telescope or telephoto lens
records.author: HeavenFox
records.storyText:
Hello HN!

As an amateur astronomer living in New York City, finding objects in the night sky has always been a huge challenge. I thought about using the smartphone's gyroscope and magnetometer, but the accuracy left a lot to be desired.

Then I learned about plate solving: given a picture of the sky, we can determine exactly where in the sky the camera was pointing by identifying the star pattern. This was a much better fit - as long as the phone and the optics are rigidly connected, we can repeatedly photograph the sky and determine the pointing direction with very high accuracy.

A lot of work was done to design an algorithm that works reliably with smartphone cameras, which have limited light sensitivity and wider field of view which includes buildings and trees. I experimented a lot with machine learning, and to my surprise, traditional CV methods actually performed better at extracting stars from the image.

The result is AstroHelm, an iOS and Android app that helps figure out where your telescope or camera is pointing, and guides you to the object of your choice. Just follow an arrow on screen, and the object will land right in your eyepiece or viewfinder. Everything happens on device, and no internet connection is required.

AstroHelm is free to use and comes with beginner-friendly objects selected for each night. Optional one time purchases unlock more objects and advanced features, such as interoperability with other astronomy software. I am also proud to partner with astronomy clubs and organizations to offer free licenses for outreach.

I hope AstroHelm can make it a little easier to discover the wonders of the night sky, and I look forward to your feedback!

records.title: Show HN: McKinley – vector editor for SF Symbols (Mac app)
records.author: AmyWorrall
records.storyText:
McKinley is a Mac app for making SF Symbols. It costs $60 (one off purchase).

SF Symbols are Apple's vector symbol format. The OS ships with thousands of them, but you can make your own for your own apps.

The recommended way to make SF Symbols is to export a template from Apple's helper app, edit it in a vector editor, then re-import it and tag all the SF Symbol specific metadata.

This process is usually a pain in the ass. SF Symbols support multiple weights -- you draw three, and Apple interpolates between them. This means that each of your weights needs to have the same paths in the same order, with the same number of points. Everything has to be converted to outlines for the interpolation to work, it doesn't render strokes.

McKinley is my attempt to save you from that. It's a vector editor that is built around the constraints of SF Symbols. You can edit your symbol while flicking between the three weights or the four colour modes. It can save SF Symbol files or sync straight to Xcode asset catalogs. You don't have to bounce between a vector editor and a symbols converter, because McKinley is both.

I'm pleased with how live previews work. I wanted to offer a preview with Apple's own renderer. But you can't load an SF Symbol in-memory at runtime. So I figured out the file format for asset catalogs, and create a temporary one and load _that_. (I blogged about how I did it: https://www.amyworrall.com/blog/previewing-sf-symbols-with-a... )

A couple of things I know people will ask:

* It's a native AppKit app (not Electron or anything cross-platform) * Sold directly from my site via Stripe, not Mac App Store. * One-time purchase. License is valid on up to 5 computers, and covers all version 1.x updates. * There's a 14 day free trial, which includes saving/exporting * It is sandboxed, notarised, and all that good stuff * No analytics or network traffic, apart from updates (handled by Sparkle) and license checking (handled by Amore).

Happy to answer any questions or dive into technical details if people want :)

records.title: Show HN: I made a browser-based instrument out of the CHOMPI CLUB source
records.author: johnwheeler
records.storyText:
A few days ago Chase Bliss open sourced the CHOMPI Club source code under an MIT license

https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49912048

so I've been working on an AU/VST3/AAX plug-in.

The plug-in includes all the samples so it's a bit heavy, so I decided to add WASM as a compilation target and compile it directly for the browser.

I've built an interactive tutorial and added UX enhancements to make editing it easier.

For those of you who don't know, the CHOMPI Club started off as a Kickstarter

https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/chompiclub/chompi-a-mag...

I bought one, and I absolutely love it. The CHOMPI development team was acqu-hired by Chase Bliss (who is a small team that makes incredible, premium guitar pedals), and for reasons unknown they decided to shelf the project and make the code open.

https://github.com/CHOMPI-Club/CHOMPI/

I think they intended other makers to build Daisy seed hardware out of it, but I want to show people how awesome an instrument this is so my goal is to not only make it accessible but to make the UX better and build tutorials around the various modes. Let people play it on the web and download it as a free plug-in if they like it.

Right now, TAPE mode is supported but TEMPO and WAVE modes are working on my development machine and I'm just testing them.

I've been working on this for the past few days all day with GPT 6 Astra Max on /ultrafast.

Right now, we're modelling an Akai S950 circuit to swap out the native CHOMPI sampler code with as an option and we've downloaded data sheets, schematics, and spent 10 hours on testing and getting it in top shape.

Have fun! Feel free to ask any questions.

- Not associated with Chase Bliss or CHOMPI Club

records.title: Show HN: Borehole – acquisition tech due diligence from a repo's Git history
records.author: nerolabs
records.storyText:
I've done technical due diligence on acquisitions for years. Most of what changes a deal is answerable from the repository: does the team review its code, does one person carry the recent work, did the licence just change, are releases cut from what's on main, do the tests run in CI. So I built a tool that reads all of that from the history and working tree, and writes a report a deal team can act on.

Seven dimensions, 100+ deterministic checks. No model writes the findings.

Every finding cites a commit, a file or a line.

What code can't settle becomes a question for a person, not a guess.

Public repositories are free: paste a GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg or SourceHut address at borehole.dev.

Private repositories never reach our servers. pip install borehole, then borehole collect . --dry-run prints exactly what would be sent: counts, paths, short matched lines, hashed author identities. Never whole files.

The technology is new, and I'd rather hear about issues here than not. The first 20 people who email support@borehole.dev with "HN beta" get a free Report key for their own private repository, in exchange for a short survey after the report.

Website: https://borehole.dev/

Example report: https://borehole.dev/r/rustdesk/rustdesk/b5d8b97

records.title: Show HN: Agents Sleep Preventer – keep your Mac awake only while AI agents work
records.author: Charlon
records.storyText:
I run several Claude Code and Codex sessions in parallel and kept coming back to either a sleeping Mac with half-finished work, or a Mac that stayed up all night because I'd left caffeinate on.

Agents Sleep Preventer hooks into the agents' own configs (Claude Code, Codex, Hermes), so it knows when each session is actually working. It keeps the Mac awake only then, lid closed included, and lets it sleep when they're done.

The menu bar lists every session by project and branch: which are working, which need you and why ("Claude needs your permission to use Bash"), and the background commands each one still runs, with a Stop button. "Sleep when done" puts the Mac to sleep once everything finishes, with an optional time limit for agents that poll forever.

It also does local push-to-talk dictation (Whisper or Parakeet, nothing leaves the Mac). Free, MIT, Rust + Swift. macOS 14+ on Apple Silicon, plus a Windows build.

records.title: Show HN: Mistis – a decoupled, E2EE protocol for mid-call user authentication
records.author: JusMKing
records.storyText:
We have built an authentication protocol enabling mid-session real-time identity verification between final users during any active communication, delivered via a proprietary decoupled channel.

System allows users to send identity verification challenges to each other on-demand during communication. The goal is to prevent identity takeover by real-time audio deepfakes.

It is inspired in 3DS credit card processing –taking away the UX nightmare; some similarities: decoupled rail for authentication, enrolment, user redirection to trusted authentication mechanism.

The method is based on cryptographic credential management, employing only open standards via a proprietary algorithm. The server relays messages and serves for message-hardening enforcement.

Cryptographic operations, source of truth and decisions are all on the client-side. The model could be considered P2P in essence and usability –despite the existence of a limited-role server as a minimal required infrastructure. Our servers do not process or store any PII.

Our first use case is applied to regular carrier mobile phone calls, and requires installing a mobile app to function. Also, the protocol can be applied and integrated into any communication.

It would be great if you’d like to have a look at it and let us know what you think. I will be here to discuss online.

You can download the app and test it (limited testers):

- Android link: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.mistis.aut...

- iOS app link: https://testflight.apple.com/join/Rb5sXpwp

Testing involves at least two users, as the method requires pairing (cryptographic credential exchange) previously to establishing a regular phone call in which to send identity verification challenges. I can volunteer for testing if you cannot find a peer tester.

If you spot a weird bug or would like to mention anything in private, please drop a line to support@mistis.tech.

Justin (Founder)

records.title: Show HN: Modrent Minecraft Hosting
records.author: withinboredom
records.storyText:
I debated doing a hn post on this with myself. But the tech behind it is pretty damn cool. And I don’t have any blog posts about it or anything like that, so. I thought I’d do that here.

My son and I play a lot of modded Minecraft. We got super annoyed with hosting servers and getting mods to stay synchronized, where even a single update on the server but forgotten on the client can result in shenanigans.

So, we worked together (he’s 12) to build modrent. Users pay for their own play time (myself funding a neighborhood of players from 17-10 is gone—but I can sponsor playtime if I want to). On the hosting side, a world starts with 8 cores and 12 gb of ram running zGC. A controller then adjusts memory pressure and cpu allocations to find the optimal configuration for the server by monitoring world metrics and detecting chunk generation, etc.

Once the world allocations is less than the cost of the players currently in the world, it starts rewarding free time to the players to reduce the actual cost per player. For example, a world that costs me 0.02 per hour with two players paying 0.02 per hour, I’d reward 30 minutes to each player so they effectively paid 0.01 per hour.

Just thought I’d share it here to discuss the tech.

records.title: Show HN: AgentiLoop Agent Mac GUI Agent Loop for macOS 14.6 or Later
records.author: macOS26
records.storyText:
Agent! originally appeared on Hacker News last April. A lot has changed since there. Recently a new feature has been developed called Auto-Pilot. It is given a goal and will not stop until the goal is reached. Think of it as tasks on steroids. What Agent does is create multi tasks. Each task is referred to as a Cycle. By default Auto-Pilot triggered by /auto [goal] do not have a time frame. Agent! is told to keep running until its goal is reached.

Auto-Pilot has a kill switch, a "Stop All" button. The user can also kill the current Cycle only using /auto stop and can also kill all using /auto stop all.

In November a user will be able to have Multiple Auto-Pilots running on the same project. And an Auto-Pilot tab will be able to automatically spawn other tabs.

Currently we are developing a Mario Kart like clone called "GoKart" written in GoDot 4. So far over 20 hours have been recorded developing and improving the game.

records.title: Show HN: PeerYeet – P2P file transfer or fail
records.author: dicroce
records.storyText:
I wanted a p2p file transfer site that didn't require you to create an account or login, didn't require you to upload your files and either established a webrtc p2p connection or just failed (no TURN relay). You're data never hits the peeryeet server.

For the hackernews audience I'll mention my other requirements: a single binary, written in C, super efficient so I can run the whole service on a very minimal VM.

Hopefully I can finally stop sharing files with myself via gmail now. :)

records.title: Show HN: Focus Tool for ADHD
records.author: talksik
records.storyText:
We live in a noisy digital world. For anyone with adhd, doing one thing at a time is the key. NOT using fancy todo managers. Win one intention at a time instead of planning, prioritizing, and juggling 100s of things.

This tool is a free, open-source application to help you stay on track. You set an intention before you work, and a big, fat overlay stays in your periphery to keep you on track.

Written purely in C, using raylib.

records.title: Show HN: Linnaeus, a daily biological taxonomy game
records.author: cartucho1
records.storyText:
What this is: Each day there's one target species, and you classify it level by level (from more general to more specific categories), with 10 seconds per choice. Faster answers score more, and there are daily and monthly leaderboards.

Why: I wanted to try out agentic coding (a bit late to the party I know). A friend gifted me a week of Claude, and this is what I got in 3 afternoons of full vibe-coding. I've had the idea for this game for a while (I'm a philosopher of biology), and this was a good toy project for it. I'd never vibe-code like this in a serious project, but wanted to see how far I could get / how good frontier models were, and I'm honestly impressed. I have mixed feelings about the whole experience, but I could have never done this so fast without it.

Stack: It's made with Svelte 5 and CF workers & D1. I've worked with both in the past and knew it's good for a little (free to host) side project like this.

Feedback welcome, especially on whether the 10 seconds feels right (I wanted to avoid people googling the categories while playing).
